newsitem.title: FRANCE: Americans in Paris favour Clinton -- just.
newsitem.headline: Americans in Paris favour Clinton -- just.

text.p: If a straw poll at one of America's most famous overseas watering holes can be believed, President Bill Clinton will beat Republican rival Bob Dole by a whisker.

The poll at Harry's Bar in Paris, an institution since 1924 when Americans did not have absentee ballots, gave Clinton 441 votes to Dole's 435, a much narrower margin than expected between the two top men fighting out Tuesday's election.
Millionaire independent candidate Ross Perot won just 35 votes from expatriate drinkers.
The bar's customers have been wrong only once: in 1976 they gave Republican candidate Gerald Ford a victory over Jimmy Carter.
Elsewhere in Paris, Americans prepared to stay up to the small hours to celebrate at hotspots around the capital.
Bars were holding all-night election bashes, the American University of Paris offered a role-playing debate and restaurants dished up special American-style menus.

The Joe Allen restaurant in the the capital's epicentre festooned its walls with campaign banners, flags and red, white and blue crepe paper and offered a fixed-price menu including California wine, buffalo wings, spare ribs and cheese cake at 350 francs ($70).

"We had to stop taking reservations, there were too many people," said a spokeswoman for the restaurant. Latecomers arriving after 1 a.m. get a drink and a breakfast of eggs and muffins for the reduced price of 100 francs ($20).
Boogie woogie and rock n' roll were on tap to accompany early returns on giant TV screens. The restaurant also planned a tombola, with the winner getting a free tip for two to New York.
At the Paris Hilton, more than 400 Americans of all persuasions paid 575 francs ($115) for election-night festivities.

After visitors including U.S. ambassador Pamela Harriman sing the national anthem, Marine Corps members were to present the colours, followed by bands playing New Orleans jazz, Cole Porter and George Gershwin tunes.
Fried chicken, nachos and apple pie a la mode were on the menu to accompany early East Coast exit polls broadcast on huge screens. A pancake breakfast was lined up to go with West Coast returns.
For those who preferred to stay at home, France's Minitel home computer network was offering regular updates on election results.
